title: Try These 3 iOS 27 Safari Settings to Get More Out of Apple's Browser
gist: iOS 27, leaving beta the following Monday, adds three Apple Intelligence-powered Safari features restricted to iPhone 15 Pro or newer: 'Notify Me' page-change tracking, 'Describe an Extension' natural-language browser extension generation, and AI-driven automatic tab organization into topic groups.

insights.claim: iOS 27 was scheduled to leave beta the Monday following this article's publication, with Siri's new standalone app and system-wide search integration expected to be the most immediately noticeable change for most users, while the new Safari features covered in the article are comparatively hidden in settings menus.
insights.speaker: Reece Rogers
insights.so_what: Confirms a concrete iOS 27 GA timeline and signals Apple is prioritizing Siri's standalone app/search overhaul as its headline consumer-facing change, with deeper AI features requiring active discovery by users.
insights.quote: When iOS 27 leaves beta on Monday, Siri AI's standalone app and smartphone search integration will likely be the most immediately obvious change for many iPhone users.

insights.claim: All three new Safari features are powered by Apple Intelligence and require an iPhone 15 Pro or newer; they are also available on iPadOS 27 and macOS 27, meaning older iPhones running iOS 27 will not get these capabilities.
insights.speaker: Reece Rogers
insights.so_what: Apple continues to segment its AI feature rollout by hardware tier (iPhone 15 Pro+), a deliberate strategy that could pressure upgrade cycles for users wanting the newest on-device AI capabilities.
insights.quote: These Safari features are powered by Apple Intelligence, which requires an iPhone 15 Pro or newer (they're also available on iPadOS 27 and macOS 27).

insights.claim: Safari's new 'Notify Me' feature lets users describe in natural language what content change to watch for on a webpage and how often to check, functioning like a general-purpose AI web-page monitor for price drops, ticket availability, or privacy policy changes rather than just retail price tracking like Chrome's price-tracking bell.
insights.speaker: Reece Rogers
insights.so_what: Positions Safari's monitoring feature as broader than Chrome's retail-only price-tracking bell, a genuine feature differentiation point in the browser market that could pull power users toward Safari for general-purpose page-change alerts.
insights.quote: While many other browsers have similar shopping features, like the price-tracking bell in Google Chrome, I appreciate how this feature stretches beyond just buying stuff. You can also use Safari to scan for ticket drops, privacy policy changes, and other content updates.

insights.claim: Safari's 'Describe an Extension' feature generates a custom browser extension from a natural-language prompt in a few seconds, with example use cases including displaying a reading-time badge, converting pages to grayscale for focus, or triggering a firework animation on tap; the reviewer found all three example prompts generated correctly and functioned as expected.
insights.speaker: Reece Rogers
insights.so_what: On-demand, natural-language-generated browser extensions represent a meaningful lowering of the technical barrier to browser customization, a feature template other browser vendors may need to match.
insights.quote: It took only a few seconds for each of those three examples to generate... everything worked as expected.

insights.claim: A new tab-organization feature can automatically group over 500 unsorted open tabs into AI-identified topic clusters within a few seconds, successfully grouping the reviewer's Wired articles and separately grouping San Francisco event pages and comedy club sites he had been browsing.
insights.speaker: Reece Rogers
insights.so_what: Demonstrates a concrete, tested AI use case (topic clustering across 500+ tabs) with real accuracy results, useful as a benchmark for on-device AI organization features versus manual tab management.
insights.quote: It did a great job of finding helpful trends in those 500+ tabs. For example, it grouped all the WIRED articles I had open and created a tab topic for upcoming San Francisco event pages and comedy clubs I was considering checking out.
